title: Opening at the Aspen festival and the L.A. Jazz Society honor
summary: Rowe introduces Candoli at the Jerome Jazz Party; they discuss the bebop set, the festival audience and his 1990 L.A. Jazz Society honor.

story.theme_name: Opening the interview: Monk Rowe's welcome and archive boilerplate
story.community_name: Opening the Hamilton College interview: introductions and boilerplate

blocks.x: We are in Aspen, Colorado at the Jerome Jazz Festival and I am extremely happy to be talking with Conte Candoli, trumpeter, and man of humor, as I’m learning quickly. And I should explain that you are in between sets here at the jazz festival, and you just shook the place up with some Charlie Parker.

Well thank you. You know I was waiting to play some bebop for the last couple of nights, and we had guys up on the stand that were familiar with that kind of music. Of course I happened to be the leader for that last set so when you’re the leader you get to sort of choose your own tunes. And I was determined to play that, whether they knew it or not.
Well I think it worked. You know the audience that comes to these things, they’re fairly settled in their tastes.

Pretty much so, but you know, I must say in their behalf that they’re in my age group too, so I go along with what they want, you know, the big band era and everything else. And it’s nice to see these people, wonderful people, supportive.
Well you’ve had a marvelous career between the big bands and bop, and just about everything else in between.

Yeah, pretty much so. I’ve been honored by the L.A. Jazz Society in 1990 and that was kind of nice, it was kind of unexpected and so apparently I fill the requirements that were necessary, to have been in L.A. for twenty years and have been playing jazz in that area for twenty years. So they honored me that particular day which was kind of nice.
I can recall reading record jackets. And I see your name come up a lot, along with your brother. And also, Conrad Gotzo. Am I pronouncing that right?
